content: The process of analysis in quality improvement (QI) must include the development of corrective strategies. These strategies should be based on a continuous cycle of monitoring, assessment, and management, as emphasized by Maier and Rhodes (2001), the Performance Improvement Subcommittee of the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (2002), and the American College of Surgeons (2006). Corrective strategies or action plans are essential components of QI, as they address identified opportunities for improvement and aim to rectify suboptimal performance. These strategies are structured interventions designed to resolve specific issues, whether they are case-specific or system-wide. Examples of corrective strategies include the implementation or modification of clinical guidelines, pathways, and protocols; targeted education through rounds, conferences, journal clubs, focused reading, case presentations, newsletters, posters, and videos; peer review presentations; and actions directed at individual providers, such as counseling, further training, or restriction of privileges. Additionally, resource enhancements, such as upgrading facilities, equipment, and communication systems, are also considered corrective measures. The quality of healthcare delivery must be recognized as equally important as its cost. Many effective corrective strategies focus on knowledge dissemination rather than expensive financial or infrastructural investments. The impact of these corrective actions must be confirmed and documented, a process often referred to as closing the loop. This ensures that measurable improvements in outcomes are achieved and can be attributed to the implemented strategies. The benefits of QI programs are well-documented, particularly in trauma care. These programs aim to reduce trauma-related mortality rates globally, especially in lowand middle-income countries. Evidence from high-income countries demonstrates that trauma QI programs consistently improve care processes, reduce mortality, and enhance patient outcomes. However, there is limited but growing evidence of their effectiveness in lowand middle-income countries. For example, in the Khon Kaen region of Thailand, a trauma QI program significantly reduced mortality rates by addressing system deficiencies and improving organization and planning without requiring high-cost investments. Peer-reviewed preventable death panels have been increasingly utilized in lowand middle-income countries to identify and address deficiencies in trauma care. For instance, in Pakistan, a peer-reviewed process identified preventable deaths and led to targeted interventions. Similarly, in Zimbabwe, a clinical audit following a mass casualty event resulted in recommendations for disaster preparedness improvements across multiple settings. In South Africa, error analysis methods adapted from aeronautical safety were used to classify and address missed injuries in trauma patients. Errors were categorized into clinical evaluation, radiological assessment, and surgical exploration, with further classification into rule-based mistakes, knowledge-based mistakes, and execution errors. These findings informed corrective actions to improve care quality. Formal outcome scoring systems, such as the Trauma and Injury Severity Score (TRISS), have been employed in various countries to identify preventable deaths and monitor the impact of QI interventions. For example, in Brazil, TRISS scoring was used to evaluate a regional prehospital program, confirming improved triage of severely injured patients to appropriate facilities. Similar methodologies have been applied in Pakistan and India to assess trauma outcomes and identify areas for improvement. In other fields, QI programs have also demonstrated success. For example, in Malawi, an audit of antibiotic usage led to the implementation of treatment guidelines, while in Malaysia, a surgical audit system improved reporting and led to the development of protocols for antibiotic prophylaxis. In obstetric care, maternal death audits have been used to identify causes of death and implement corrective actions, resulting in improved maternal outcomes. Overall, QI programs have proven to be effective in improving care processes, reducing mortality, and enhancing patient outcomes across various settings. Further efforts to promote and implement QI programs globally, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, are warranted to address existing deficiencies in healthcare delivery.
